articles.title: The Visitor review – existential Lithuania-set homecoming drama leaves everything in limbo
articles.summary: This portrait by Vytautas Katkus of a man contemplating his recent fatherhood and his own father is steeped in ennui and ends up drifting. At one point in this Nordic-Baltic homecoming film, Danielius (Darius Šilėnas) refuses an invite for beachfront karaoke, preferring to watch from behind a…
body: Little tangible is disclosed. Danielius is a thirtysomething father who skipped the funeral of his own dad the year before. Preparing the flat to go on the market, he walks the dog of his neighbour, Vismante (Vismantė Ruzgaitė), hangs speculatively at beach gatherings and falls asleep in pine forests. Ice-cream is eaten at every available opportunity. He’s not alienated exactly, but somewhat out of step. As he looks for new anchorage, even the film seems to question whether Danielius has sufficient main character energy: it periodically drifts to follow another resident, Tomas (Rokas Siaurusaitis), who is caring for his grandmother over the way.

articles.title: Marching in the Dark review – rural Indian widows show stunning resilience as they battle poverty and taboos
articles.summary: Kinshuk Surjan’s documentary follows women in dire financial straits whose bereavement compounds their social plight, which they confront together. Out in rural India, a crisis casts a dark cloud over the seemingly tranquil vistas of wheat fields and soy farms.
body: Sanjivani, a woman in her 30s, is one such case. Eight years after her husband killed himself, she has taken over some of the farming responsibilities, along with other odd jobs, to provide for her two children. The camera rarely finds her at rest; Sanjivani not only works in the fields but also performs domestic labour for her extended family – cooking, cleaning and doing laundry. Her resilience is stunning to witness, but even more impressive is the emotional support provided by a tight-knit network of other widows. Together, the women gather for counselling sessions where they can freely discuss their emotional, physical and financial issues.

articles.title: ‘A bit like meditation’: why Saw is my feelgood movie
articles.summary: The latest in our series of writers picking their go-to comfort films is a grimy and gory trip back to the start of a surprisingly uplifting torture porn franchise. I was petsitting recently for a white suburban family, with the typical streaming habits therein.
body: I was obsessed with the Saw franchise well before I ever saw it. At 11, as Jigsaw puppets became Halloween costumes, I went to bed each night convinced Jigsaw was going to scoop me up in a van because the word “hell”a popped into my head. By 13, I looked up every film on Wikipedia and read through each trap with terrified excitement. By 14, I drank my first can of Stella and typed Saw II into YouTube, watching it in 12 installments. It was utterly horrifying. And so, so, so much fun.

I am now 31 and have seen every film so many times I could count on both hands – which Jigsaw would sever finger by finger – how many times I’ve seen them. Somewhere along the way, Saw became my feel-good film.

articles.title: Disciples review – fresh-faced boys are sucked into a nightmare of extremism in India
articles.summary: A prestigious school in the holy city of Varanasi and its controversial, dogmatic teachings are the subject of this shocking documentary. The effect of political and religious indoctrination on young minds resembles a slow-release poison.
body: The film opens with controversial speeches made by the school’s spiritual leader, Guru Avimuktesh, who advocates the abolition of religious freedom, and for Indian Muslims to either convert to Hinduism or leave for Pakistan. A prominent Hindu figure with a large following, he personally oversees the entrance exam, a sequence captured in dynamic handheld shots. While boys take the test, their parents look on with apprehension and anxiety; to be accepted would be an honour, not only for their child but for the whole family.

For those who do get in to Vidya Mutth, what follows is far from a glorious, enlightening experience. Focusing on two new entrants called Satyarth and Hari, the film documents their daily routines, which largely revolve around Sanskrit classes. The learning of this ancient script, supposedly to maintain a linguistic tradition, is actually in service of religious dogmatism; in between classes, Guru Avimuktesh continues to preach Islamophobic and casteist ideas, packaged as fact.

The effect of political and religious indoctrination on young minds resembles a slow-release poison.

body: WME is handling domestic rights on the thriller, which marks Eugene Kotlyarenko’s eighth feature.
The key crew includes Sean Price Williams, the topnotch cinematographer of “Good Time,” “The Sweet East” and “The Moment,” among others.

“‘Vintage Violence’ was made with lots of enthusiasm and cinephilia from everyone involved, so it’s great to work with Best Friend Forever, a company brimming with both those qualities,” said Kotlyarenko said. “Most importantly, we have the same goal in mind: for audiences all over the world to get rocked by this movie.”

The film reteams Kotlyarenko with producers Alex Hughes and Riccardo Maddalosso of Spacemaker Productions, which also backed ’s “Spree” and “The Code.” The company’s credits also include James Gray’s “Armageddon Time” and Sebastián Silva’s “Rotting in the Sun,” among others. Japan’s Barravento, whose credits include “Onoda: 10,000 Nights in the Jungle,” and Mam Film, behind “Love Life,” are co-producing.

articles.title: Vietnamese Found-Footage Horror Hit ‘Lau Chu Hoa: The Deadliest Mansion’ Heads to North American Theaters (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.summary: Vietnamese found-footage horror film “Lầu Chú Hoả: The Deadliest Mansion” is opening in North American theaters on Sept. 4, with Mockingbird Pictures placing the title across AMC, Regal and Cinemark circuits.
body: “Lầu Chú Hoả: The Deadliest Mansion” was produced by Runup Vietnam alongside South Korea’s Hive Media Corp, marking the Korean company’s first production investment outside its home market. Hive has backed several of Korea’s biggest recent releases, including “12.12: The Day,” “Inside Men,” “The Man Standing Next” and “Harbin,” along with the found-footage horror title “Gonjiam: Haunted Asylum,” which drew more than 2.6 million admissions in South Korea.

“Found footage has the power to make audiences feel as though they are experiencing the horror themselves,” said producer Lee Jin Sung. “Working with Hive Media Corp allowed us to bring that experience to a uniquely Vietnamese legend while preserving the identity and atmosphere that make the story distinctive.”
Mockingbird Pictures is overseeing the North American theatrical rollout as part of its broader effort to bring Vietnamese commercial films to international audiences.

articles.title: Dutch broadcaster Avrotros pulls out of 2027 Eurovision Song Contest
articles.summary: It says contest can no longer be considered neutral while a participating country remains involved in a large-scale military conflict.
body: In a statement, external released on Monday, the broadcaster said the decision was due to a lack of clarity from organisers - the Eurovision Broadcasting Union (EBU) - over assessing which countries could compete.

Avrotros added: "The severe humanitarian suffering in Gaza and the ongoing restrictions on press freedom have contributed to increasing divisions surrounding the Eurovision Song Contest in recent years."

Earlier this month, the EBU updated their rules to state that if a country involved in an armed conflict wins the competition, it will be ineligible to host it the following year. But Avrotros said those changes "do not provide sufficient confidence that ‌the ⁠independent and neutral character of the Eurovision Song Contest has been restored."
The broadcaster's withdrawal from this year's contest in Burgas, Bulgaria, does not necessarily rule out Dutch participation in Eurovision 2027.

articles.title: Race Across the World star dies year after son
articles.summary: Former TV contestant, Jo Gardiner, 61, dies of cancer one year after her son's death in a crash.
body: A former Race Across the World contestant has died, a year after her son and co-star's death in a car crash.
Jo Gardiner, 61, died "following a long and courageous battle with cancer", her family said.
Gardiner, a physiotherapist from Manchester, travelled across South America with her son Sam in the second series of the BBC show, which aired in 2020.
Her family said she was "one of a kind" who "lived fully, fiercely and never did anything by halves".

articles.title: Venice Adds Gaza Doc ‘Naza’ to Competition
articles.summary: Directed by 'No Other Land' filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, the doc explores Israeli military killings of Palestinian civilians in Gaza.
body: The Venice Film Festival has added Naza, a politically-charged documentary from No Other Land filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor to its competition line-up for this year.
The documentary claims to reveal in detail “the systems behind Israel’s calculated mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza.”
The doc will have its world premiere in Venice on Sept. 10. It is the only feature documentary picked for competition this year.

Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor are two of the four co-directors of No Other Land, the Oscar-winning documentary that chronicled violent evictions of Palestinians from their homes in the occupied West Bank.
